chapter_text:
CHAPTER 16 — मानो हि महतां धनम् (MANO HI MAHATAM DHANAM)

Introduction — प्रस्तावना

The title of this lesson, मानो हि महतां धनम्, means "self-respect indeed is the wealth of the great." The word मानः here does not mean pride in the negative sense; it means आत्मगौरवम् — self-respect, the quiet inner dignity of a person who will not sell his conscience for any price. Its close synonym is स्वाभिमानः (स्व + अभिमानः, "honour of one's own self"). Sanskrit literature repeatedly teaches that noble people (महान्तः) count this dignity as their true wealth: gold can be stolen, kingdoms can be conquered, but self-respect can only be surrendered — and the noble never surrender it. At the same time the tradition draws a sharp line between मानः (self-respect) and अहङ्कारः (arrogance): the self-respecting person honours others as he honours himself, while the arrogant person demands honour and insults others. In this lesson (NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit, Course 309) we read an original Sanskrit story of a chieftain who chose forest hardship over gilded servitude, study five famous public-domain नीति verses on honour and dignity with their शब्दार्थ and अन्वय, reflect on the difference between स्वाभिमान and अहङ्कार, and draw grammar — सन्धि, समास, विभक्ति and लकार — from the text.

कथा — वीरवर्मणः स्वाभिमानः (The Story of Viravarman's Self-Respect)

आसीत् पुरा गिरिदुर्गे वीरवर्मा नाम नृपतिः। सः अल्पस्य राज्यस्य अधिपतिः आसीत्, किन्तु तस्य मानः पर्वतात् अपि उन्नतः आसीत्। एकदा चण्डसेनः नाम बलवान् सम्राट् तं देशम् अजयत्। सः दूतं प्रेषितवान् — "यदि वीरवर्मा मम सभायाम् आगत्य शिरः नमयति, दासभावं च स्वीकरोति, तर्हि अहं तस्मै सुवर्णं प्रासादं विशालं राज्यं च दास्यामि" इति।

वीरवर्मा शान्तं हसित्वा अवदत् — "धनं नश्यति, प्रासादः शीर्यते, राज्यं हस्तात् हस्तं गच्छति। मानः एव महतां धनम्। स्वाभिमानं विक्रीय लब्धं राज्यं दास्यम् एव भवति, न राज्यम्।" इति उक्त्वा सः राज्यं त्यक्त्वा सपरिवारः वनम् अगच्छत्।

वने तस्य जीवनं कठिनम् आसीत्। सः तृणधान्यस्य रोटिकां खादति स्म, भूमौ शेते स्म। तथापि तस्य मुखे शान्तिः आसीत्। त्रिवारं सम्राजः दूताः अधिकं सुवर्णं गृहीत्वा आगच्छन्, त्रिवारं च सः सविनयम् एव निराकरोत् — "भोः, युष्माकं स्वामिने मम प्रणामाः सन्तु। किन्तु मम उत्तरं तदेव अस्ति" इति।

वीरवर्मा स्वाभिमानी आसीत्, न तु अहङ्कारी। सः वृद्धं गुरुं दृष्ट्वा प्रणमति स्म, कुम्भकारं कृषकं च आदरेण सम्भाषते स्म। एकदा तस्य अश्वः कृषकस्य क्षेत्रम् अमर्दयत्। वीरवर्मा स्वयं कृषकसमीपं गत्वा क्षमां याचितवान्, स्वस्य अन्तिमम् अङ्गुलीयकं च तस्मै दत्तवान्।

इदं श्रुत्वा चण्डसेनः विस्मितः अभवत् — "यः दरिद्रः अपि कृषकात् क्षमां याचते, स्वमानं तु सुवर्णेन अपि न विक्रीणाति, सः एव सत्यं महान्" इति चिन्तयित्वा सः स्वयं वनम् अगच्छत्, निःशर्तं तस्य राज्यं प्रत्यर्पितवान्, मित्रतां च अयाचत। वीरवर्मा समभावेन मित्रतां स्वीकृतवान्। एवं मानेन एव सः धनं राज्यं यशः च पुनः अलभत।

शब्दार्थ (Word meanings of the story): गिरिदुर्गम् = hill fort; नृपतिः = king; अधिपतिः = lord, ruler; उन्नतः = high, lofty; सम्राट् = emperor; अजयत् = conquered; दूतः = messenger, envoy; सभायाम् = in the court; शिरः नमयति = bows the head; दासभावः = attitude of servitude; सुवर्णम् = gold; प्रासादः = palace; दास्यामि = I shall give; नश्यति = perishes; शीर्यते = withers, crumbles; विक्रीय = having sold; दास्यम् = servitude, slavery; त्यक्त्वा = having abandoned; सपरिवारः = with his family; तृणधान्यम् = wild grass-grain; रोटिका = bread; भूमौ = on the ground; शेते स्म = used to sleep; त्रिवारम् = three times; सविनयम् = politely, with humility; निराकरोत् = refused; प्रणामाः = salutations; कुम्भकारः = potter; कृषकः = farmer; अश्वः = horse; क्षेत्रम् = field; अमर्दयत् = trampled; क्षमा = forgiveness, pardon; याचितवान् = begged, asked for; अङ्गुलीयकम् = ring; दरिद्रः = poor; विस्मितः = amazed; निःशर्तम् = unconditionally; प्रत्यर्पितवान् = returned, gave back; मित्रता = friendship; समभावेन = with equanimity, as an equal; यशः = fame, glory.

English translation of the story: Long ago there was a king named Viravarman in a hill fort. He was lord of a small kingdom, but his self-respect was loftier than the mountain itself. Once a powerful emperor named Chandasena conquered that region. He sent an envoy: "If Viravarman comes to my court, bows his head and accepts servitude, I shall give him gold, a palace and a vast kingdom." Viravarman smiled calmly and said: "Wealth perishes, palaces crumble, kingdoms pass from hand to hand. Self-respect alone is the wealth of the great. A kingdom obtained by selling one's self-respect is only servitude, not a kingdom." So saying, he abandoned his kingdom and went to the forest with his family. Life in the forest was hard: he ate bread of wild grass-grain and slept on the bare ground, yet there was peace on his face. Three times the emperor's envoys came with ever more gold, and three times he refused — politely: "Sirs, my salutations to your master; but my answer remains the same." Viravarman was self-respecting, not arrogant: he bowed to his aged teacher, spoke respectfully to the potter and the farmer. Once his horse trampled a farmer's field; Viravarman himself went to the farmer, begged forgiveness, and gave him his last ring. Hearing all this, Chandasena was amazed: "One who, though poor, begs pardon of a farmer, yet will not sell his honour even for gold — he alone is truly great." The emperor himself went to the forest, returned the kingdom unconditionally, and asked for friendship. Viravarman accepted the friendship as an equal. Thus by self-respect alone he regained wealth, kingdom and fame.

Moral (नीतिः): Honour kept in hardship outshines riches gained in humiliation. True self-respect walks together with humility and courtesy — Viravarman refuses an emperor yet apologises to a farmer. And in the end, the world bows to the one who would not sell his dignity.

नीतिश्लोकाः — Five classic verses on honour and dignity (शब्दार्थ, अन्वय, translation)

1) निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु
   लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् ।
   अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा
   न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥ (भर्तृहरिः, नीतिशतकम्)
   शब्दार्थ: निन्दन्तु = let them blame; नीतिनिपुणाः = those skilled in policy/ethics; स्तुवन्तु = let them praise; लक्ष्मीः = the goddess of fortune, wealth; समाविशतु = let her come/enter; यथेष्टम् = as she pleases; अद्य एव = this very day; मरणम् = death; युगान्तरे = after an age; न्याय्यात् पथः = from the just path; प्रविचलन्ति = swerve, deviate; पदम् = a step; धीराः = the steadfast, the resolute.
   अन्वय: नीतिनिपुणाः निन्दन्तु यदि वा स्तुवन्तु, लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु वा यथेष्टं गच्छतु, मरणम् अद्य एव अस्तु युगान्तरे वा — धीराः न्याय्यात् पथः पदं न प्रविचलन्ति।
   Translation: Let the masters of policy blame or praise; let fortune come or leave as she pleases; let death come this very day or after an age — the steadfast do not swerve even a single step from the path of justice.

2) कुसुमस्तबकस्येव द्वयी वृत्तिर्मनस्विनः ।
   मूर्ध्नि वा सर्वलोकस्य शीर्यते वन एव वा ॥ (भर्तृहरिः, नीतिशतकम्)
   शब्दार्थ: कुसुमस्तबकस्य = of a cluster of flowers; इव = like; द्वयी = twofold; वृत्तिः = course, way of life; मनस्विनः = of the self-respecting, high-minded person; मूर्ध्नि = on the head; सर्वलोकस्य = of the whole world; शीर्यते = withers away; वने = in the forest; एव = alone, only.
   अन्वय: मनस्विनः कुसुमस्तबकस्य इव द्वयी वृत्तिः — सर्वलोकस्य मूर्ध्नि वा (तिष्ठति), वने एव वा शीर्यते।
   Translation: The self-respecting person, like a cluster of flowers, has only two courses: either he rests on the head of the whole world, or he withers away in the forest — he never lets himself be trampled underfoot.

3) वरं प्राणपरित्यागो मानभङ्गेन जीवनात् ।
   प्राणत्यागे क्षणं दुःखं मानभङ्गे दिने दिने ॥ (नीतिवचनम्)
   शब्दार्थ: वरम् = better; प्राणपरित्यागः = giving up of life; मानभङ्गेन = with honour broken; जीवनात् = than living; प्राणत्यागे = in giving up life; क्षणम् = for a moment; दुःखम् = pain; मानभङ्गे = when honour is broken; दिने दिने = day after day.
   अन्वय: मानभङ्गेन जीवनात् प्राणपरित्यागः वरम्; प्राणत्यागे क्षणं दुःखम्, मानभङ्गे (तु) दिने दिने (दुःखम्)।
   Translation: Better to give up life than to live on with honour broken; in giving up life the pain lasts a moment, but with broken honour there is pain day after day.

4) गुणैरुत्तमतां याति नोच्चैरासनसंस्थितः ।
   प्रासादशिखरस्थोऽपि काकः किं गरुडायते ॥ (नीतिवचनम्)
   शब्दार्थ: गुणैः = by virtues; उत्तमताम् = greatness, excellence; याति = attains; न = not; उच्चैः आसनसंस्थितः = by sitting on a high seat; प्रासादशिखरस्थः = perched on the top of a palace; अपि = even; काकः = a crow; किम् = does it?; गरुडायते = become Garuda (the king of birds).
   अन्वय: (जनः) गुणैः उत्तमतां याति, न उच्चैः आसनसंस्थितः; प्रासादशिखरस्थः अपि काकः किं गरुडायते?
   Translation: One attains greatness by virtues, not by occupying a high seat; does a crow become Garuda merely by perching on a palace tower? True honour rests on merit, never on position.

5) गौरवं प्राप्यते दानात् न तु वित्तस्य सञ्चयात् ।
   स्थितिरुच्चैः पयोदानां पयोधीनामधः स्थितिः ॥ (सुभाषितम्)
   शब्दार्थ: गौरवम् = honour, dignity; प्राप्यते = is obtained; दानात् = from giving; न तु = but not; वित्तस्य = of wealth; सञ्चयात् = from hoarding; स्थितिः = position, place; उच्चैः = high; पयोदानाम् = of the clouds (givers of water); पयोधीनाम् = of the oceans (holders of water); अधः = below.
   अन्वय: गौरवं दानात् प्राप्यते, न तु वित्तस्य सञ्चयात्; पयोदानां स्थितिः उच्चैः, पयोधीनां (तु) स्थितिः अधः।
   Translation: Honour is won by giving, not by hoarding wealth: the clouds, which give water, stand high in the sky; the oceans, which hoard water, lie below.

मानः च अहङ्कारः च — Self-respect versus arrogance

Self-respect (मानः / स्वाभिमानः) and arrogance (अहङ्कारः / गर्वः) may look similar from outside — both refuse to bend — but they are opposites within. स्वाभिमानः is rooted in values: the self-respecting person refuses only what is unjust or degrading, and he gives every other person the same dignity he claims for himself. That is why Viravarman could refuse an emperor and yet bow to his teacher and apologise to a farmer. अहङ्कारः is rooted in comparison: the arrogant person wants to stand above others, demands honour without earning it (the crow on the palace tower), insults the weak, and can never admit a mistake. The tests are simple: self-respect can say "I was wrong, forgive me"; arrogance cannot. Self-respect bears hardship with a calm face; arrogance bears no slight, however small. Self-respect is the wealth of the great; arrogance is the poverty of the small. Wisdom also warns the other way: dignity must not harden into stubbornness over trifles. The धीर of Bhartrhari's verse stands firm on the न्याय्य पथ — the just path — not on every whim of ego.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the text

(A) सन्धिः: मानः + हि → मानो हि (विसर्ग-सन्धिः: the visarga becomes ओ before a soft consonant — the very title of our chapter). Likewise न + अस्ति → नास्ति (दीर्घ-सन्धिः, अ + अ = आ); अद्य + एव → अद्यैव (वृद्धि-सन्धिः, अ + ए = ऐ); गुणैः + उत्तमताम् → गुणैरुत्तमताम् (विसर्ग-सन्धिः, ः → र्); प्रासादशिखरस्थः + अपि → प्रासादशिखरस्थोऽपि (विसर्ग-सन्धिः with पूर्वरूप, marked by the avagraha ऽ); च + एव → चैव. Splitting such forms back (सन्धि-विच्छेदः) is an essential reading skill.

(B) समासः: प्राणपरित्यागः = प्राणानां परित्यागः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः, "abandonment of life"); मानभङ्गः = मानस्य भङ्गः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः); नीतिनिपुणः = नीतिषु निपुणः (सप्तमी-तत्पुरुषः, "skilled in ethics"); कुसुमस्तबकः = कुसुमानां स्तबकः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः); स्वाभिमानः = स्वस्य अभिमानः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः); गिरिदुर्गम् = गिरौ दुर्गम् (सप्तमी-तत्पुरुषः); यथेष्टम् = इष्टम् अनतिक्रम्य (अव्ययीभावः, "as desired"); सर्वलोकः = सर्वः च असौ लोकः (कर्मधारयः).

(C) विभक्तिः: महताम् (महत्, षष्ठी बहुवचनम् — "of the great", as in the title); गुणैः (तृतीया बहुवचनम् — "by virtues"); जीवनात् (पञ्चमी एकवचनम् — "than living", the ablative of comparison with वरम्); वने, मूर्ध्नि, सभायाम्, भूमौ (सप्तमी — place "in/on"); दिने दिने (सप्तमी with वीप्सा, repetition — "day after day"); तस्मै, स्वामिने (चतुर्थी — "to him / to the master", recipient of giving); कृषकस्य, सर्वलोकस्य (षष्ठी — possession).

(D) लकारः: याति, नश्यति, शीर्यते, गच्छति — लट् (present); निन्दन्तु, स्तुवन्तु, समाविशतु, गच्छतु, अस्तु, सन्तु — लोट् (imperative/benediction, very frequent in verse 1); दास्यामि — लृट् (future, "I shall give"); अगच्छत्, अजयत्, अमर्दयत्, अवदत् — लङ् (past); भवेत्, ब्रूयात् — विधिलिङ् (should/ought).

SUMMARY (सारांशः)

In this chapter you learned that मानः — self-respect, आत्मगौरवम् — is the true wealth of the great, a wealth no conqueror can seize. The story of Viravarman showed self-respect in action: he refused gold, palace and kingdom offered at the price of servitude, endured forest hardship with a calm face, and yet remained humble — bowing to his teacher and apologising to a farmer — until his dignity itself won back all he had lost. Five classic verses deepened the theme: Bhartrhari's धीराः who never swerve from the just path whatever fortune or critics do; the मनस्विन् who, like a flower-cluster, either adorns the world's head or withers in the forest; the नीति maxim that a moment's pain of death is better than the daily pain of broken honour; the crow that does not become Garuda by perching on a palace; and the clouds that stand high because they give. You learned to distinguish स्वाभिमानः from अहङ्कारः — firmness on the just path versus vanity of ego — and you drew grammar from the text: विसर्ग and other सन्धि (मानो हि = मानः + हि), तत्पुरुष and अव्ययीभाव समास, the विभक्ति of key words (महताम्, गुणैः, जीवनात्, दिने दिने), and the लकार of the verbs (लट्, लोट्, लङ्, लृट्, विधिलिङ्). Memorise these verses — they are armour for the character.

topics.description: An original Sanskrit story: chieftain Viravarman refuses emperor Chandasena's gold, palace and kingdom offered at the price of bowing into servitude, chooses forest hardship, remains courteous and humble, and finally wins back everything through his unsold dignity.

chapter_summary.title: मानो हि महतां धनम् — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit (309) summary for Chapter 16 explains why self-respect (मानः / स्वाभिमानः) is called the wealth of the great. It retells the story of Viravarman who refused an empire offered at the price of servitude, presents five classic niti verses on honour with their meanings, contrasts self-respect with arrogance, and gathers the grammar of the chapter.
