sections.heading: What मानः means and why it is wealth
bullets: मानः in this chapter means आत्मगौरवम् — self-respect, inner dignity — not pride in the negative sense; its synonym is स्वाभिमानः (स्व + अभिमानः).
Gold can be stolen and kingdoms conquered, but self-respect can only be surrendered — so the great count it as their real, imperishable wealth.
The maxim मानो हि महतां धनम् — 'self-respect indeed is the wealth of the great' — gives the chapter its title and its theme.

sections.heading: The story of Viravarman
bullets: Emperor Chandasena offers Viravarman gold, a palace and a vast kingdom if he will bow in court and accept दासभावः (servitude).
Viravarman refuses — 'a kingdom bought by selling self-respect is only servitude' — and goes to the forest, eating grass-grain bread and sleeping on the ground with a calm face.
Three times envoys return with more gold; three times he refuses, always politely, sending salutations to their master.
His self-respect is not arrogance: he bows to his teacher, speaks respectfully to potter and farmer, and begs a farmer's pardon when his horse tramples the field, giving his last ring.
Amazed that a man who apologises to a farmer will not sell his honour for gold, the emperor returns the kingdom unconditionally and seeks his friendship.

sections.heading: The five niti verses
bullets: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणाः (Bhartrhari): praise or blame, fortune or ruin, death today or after an age — the धीराः never swerve a step from the just path.
कुसुमस्तबकस्येव (Bhartrhari): the self-respecting man, like a flower-cluster, either adorns the head of the world or withers in the forest — never underfoot.
वरं प्राणपरित्यागो मानभङ्गेन जीवनात्: death's pain lasts a moment; the pain of broken honour returns day after day.
गुणैरुत्तमतां याति: greatness comes from virtues, not from a high seat — a crow on a palace tower does not become Garuda.
गौरवं प्राप्यते दानात्: honour is won by giving, not hoarding — clouds that give water stand high; oceans that hoard it lie below.

sections.heading: Self-respect versus arrogance
bullets: स्वाभिमानः is rooted in values: it refuses only the unjust and gives every person the same dignity it claims — so Viravarman refuses an emperor yet apologises to a farmer.
अहङ्कारः is rooted in comparison: it demands unearned honour, insults the weak, and can never say 'I was wrong'.
The simple tests: self-respect can apologise and bears hardship calmly; arrogance cannot apologise and bears no slight.
Wisdom's balance: dignity must not harden into stubbornness over trifles — the धीर stands firm on the just path, not on every whim of ego.

sections.heading: Grammar from the chapter
bullets: सन्धि: मानः + हि = मानो हि (विसर्ग-सन्धि); न + अस्ति = नास्ति (दीर्घ); अद्य + एव = अद्यैव (वृद्धि); प्रासादशिखरस्थः + अपि = प्रासादशिखरस्थोऽपि (पूर्वरूप with avagraha).
समास: प्राणपरित्यागः = प्राणानां परित्यागः and मानभङ्गः = मानस्य भङ्गः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष); नीतिनिपुणः = नीतिषु निपुणः (सप्तमी-तत्पुरुष); यथेष्टम् (अव्ययीभाव).
विभक्ति: महताम् = षष्ठी बहुवचन ('of the great'); गुणैः = तृतीया ('by virtues'); जीवनात् = पञ्चमी of comparison; वने / मूर्ध्नि / दिने दिने = सप्तमी.
लकार: याति / शीर्यते = लट्; निन्दन्तु / स्तुवन्तु / अस्तु = लोट्; अगच्छत् / अजयत् = लङ्; दास्यामि = लृट्; ब्रूयात् / भवेत् = विधिलिङ्.

key_takeaways: मानः (self-respect, आत्मगौरवम्) is the one wealth that cannot be stolen — only surrendered; hence मानो हि महतां धनम्.
Viravarman's story shows that a kingdom bought by selling dignity is servitude, and that dignity kept in hardship finally wins back everything.
True self-respect walks with humility: refuse the emperor's unjust condition, yet bow to the teacher and apologise to the farmer.
Bhartrhari's धीराः never swerve from the just path, whatever critics, fortune or death may do.
Greatness comes from गुण (virtue) and दान (giving), not from a high seat or a full treasury — the crow is no Garuda, the cloud stands above the ocean.
अहङ्कारः is the counterfeit of मानः: it demands honour instead of earning it and can never admit a mistake.
From the grammar: मानो हि is a विसर्ग-सन्धि of मानः + हि, महताम् is षष्ठी बहुवचन, and निन्दन्तु / स्तुवन्तु are लोट् लकार.

glossary.definition: Self-respect, honour, inner dignity (आत्मगौरवम्); in this chapter the true wealth of the great — not arrogance.
Self-respect; स्वस्य अभिमानः — rightful honour of one's own self, upheld without insulting others.
Arrogance, egotism; the counterfeit of self-respect that demands unearned honour and cannot admit a mistake.
Dignity of the self; the sense of self-worth that noble people refuse to sell at any price.
The attitude or condition of servitude; what the emperor demanded of Viravarman in exchange for wealth.
The steadfast, resolute person who does not swerve from the just path whatever praise, blame, fortune or death may come.
A high-minded, self-respecting person; like a flower-cluster he rests on the world's head or withers in the forest.
The breaking of one's honour (मानस्य भङ्गः); living with it is called worse than a moment's pain of death.
The giving up of life (प्राणानां परित्यागः, षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष); preferred by the niti verse to a life of daily humiliation.
Honour, weight, dignity; won by giving (दानात्), as the high-standing clouds show, not by hoarding.
One skilled in ethics or policy (नीतिषु निपुणः, सप्तमी-तत्पुरुष); whose praise or blame leaves the steadfast unmoved.
'Acts like Garuda / becomes Garuda' — a denominative verb used of the crow that merely perches on a palace tower.
Sandhi of the visarga: e.g. मानः + हि = मानो हि, where ः becomes ओ before a soft consonant.
A compound whose first member carries a genitive sense, e.g. मानभङ्गः = मानस्य भङ्गः.
The imperative/benedictive verb form, e.g. निन्दन्तु 'let them blame', स्तुवन्तु 'let them praise', अस्तु 'let it be'.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — मानो हि महतां धनम् (NIOS Sanskrit 309, Chapter 16)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write Sanskrit words in Devanagari and explanations in English. Refer to the story of Viravarman and the five niti verses of the lesson where needed.

questions.question: मानो हि महतां धनम् — इति वाक्ये 'महताम्' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः? (In the title, what does 'महताम्' mean?)
questions.explanation: महताम् is षष्ठी बहुवचन of महत् — 'of the great (people)'.

questions.question: According to Bhartrhari's verse निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणाः..., what do the धीराः never do?
options: Swerve a step from the just path
questions.answer: Swerve a step from the just path
questions.explanation: न्याय्यात् पथः पदं न प्रविचलन्ति — they do not deviate even a step from the path of justice.

questions.question: True or False: In the story, Viravarman finally accepted the emperor's gold on the third visit of the envoys.
questions.explanation: All three times he politely refused; he never accepted the gold. The emperor later returned the kingdom unconditionally.

questions.question: सन्धिं कुरुत: मानः + हि = ____ ।
questions.explanation: विसर्ग-सन्धि: the visarga of मानः becomes ओ before the soft consonant ह् — मानो हि, the chapter's title.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of: नृपतिः, दासभावः, अङ्गुलीयकम्, क्षमा, यशः.
questions.answer: नृपतिः = king; दासभावः = attitude/condition of servitude; अङ्गुलीयकम् = ring; क्षमा = forgiveness, pardon; यशः = fame, glory.
questions.explanation: All five words occur in the story of Viravarman.

questions.question: What condition did emperor Chandasena attach to his offer of gold, palace and kingdom, and how did Viravarman answer in one sentence?
questions.answer: The condition was that Viravarman must come to the imperial court, bow his head and accept दासभावः (servitude). Viravarman answered: 'Wealth perishes, palaces crumble, kingdoms change hands — self-respect alone is the wealth of the great; a kingdom bought by selling self-respect is only servitude, not a kingdom' — and he refused.
questions.explanation: The offer tested whether dignity could be bought; the refusal states the chapter's central maxim.

questions.question: Write the अन्वय and simple English meaning of: वरं प्राणपरित्यागो मानभङ्गेन जीवनात् । प्राणत्यागे क्षणं दुःखं मानभङ्गे दिने दिने ॥
questions.answer: अन्वय: मानभङ्गेन जीवनात् प्राणपरित्यागः वरम्; प्राणत्यागे क्षणं दुःखम्, मानभङ्गे तु दिने दिने दुःखम्। Meaning: Better to give up life than to live with broken honour; giving up life pains for a moment, but broken honour pains day after day.
questions.explanation: जीवनात् is the ablative of comparison with वरम्; दिने दिने expresses repetition (day after day).

questions.question: Read and answer: एकदा वीरवर्मणः अश्वः कृषकस्य क्षेत्रम् अमर्दयत्। वीरवर्मा स्वयं कृषकसमीपं गत्वा क्षमां याचितवान्, स्वस्य अन्तिमम् अङ्गुलीयकं च तस्मै दत्तवान्। (a) What wrong had occurred and who was harmed? (b) What two things did Viravarman do? (c) What does this episode prove about the difference between स्वाभिमानः and अहङ्कारः?
questions.answer: (a) Viravarman's horse trampled a farmer's field, harming the poor farmer. (b) Viravarman himself went to the farmer, begged forgiveness (क्षमां याचितवान्), and gave him his last ring as compensation. (c) It proves his firmness before the emperor was self-respect, not arrogance: a स्वाभिमानी can bow, apologise and make amends to even the humblest person, while an अहङ्कारी could never admit a fault — dignity for him includes giving others their dignity.
questions.explanation: The episode is the story's key evidence that self-respect and humility coexist.

questions.question: Explain the simile of Bhartrhari's verse कुसुमस्तबकस्येव द्वयी वृत्तिर्मनस्विनः — मूर्ध्नि वा सर्वलोकस्य शीर्यते वन एव वा — and connect it to Viravarman's choice in the story.
questions.answer: Bhartrhari compares the मनस्वी (self-respecting person) to a cluster of flowers, which has only two possible fates: either it is placed on the head of the whole world (worn with honour), or it withers away unseen in the forest. What it never does is lie trampled in the middle — half-honoured, half-degraded. So too the self-respecting person either lives with full honour or accepts obscurity and hardship, but never a life of humiliation. Viravarman lives this verse: offered wealth with humiliation attached, he chooses the forest — literally the flower's second fate — eating grass-bread and sleeping on the ground rather than 'adorning' a court as a servant. And as the verse hints, such a flower's fragrance spreads: his dignity finally brings the world (even the emperor) to honour him, restoring him to 'the head of the world'.
questions.explanation: The two वृत्ति of the flower map exactly to the hero's alternatives: honoured rule or dignified exile — never servitude.

questions.question: 'Self-respect is the wealth of the great, but arrogance is the poverty of the small.' Evaluate this statement using the chapter — the story, at least two verses, and the tests that distinguish मानः from अहङ्कारः. Add one example from a student's daily life.
questions.answer: The chapter defines मानः as आत्मगौरवम् — dignity rooted in values — and calls it wealth because it cannot be stolen, only surrendered; Viravarman loses gold, palace and kingdom yet remains 'rich', and in the end this unsold dignity buys back everything. The verses support this: the धीराः of निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणाः hold the just path against praise, blame, fortune and death; गुणैरुत्तमतां याति warns that a crow on a palace tower is still a crow — honour rests on merit, not position; गौरवं दानात् adds that honour is earned by giving, not hoarding. Arrogance is the counterfeit: it demands honour without merit, insults the weak, and cannot apologise — a poverty of character however rich the purse. The tests: self-respect can say 'I was wrong' (Viravarman before the farmer) and bears hardship calmly (peace on his face in the forest); arrogance can do neither. Student example: refusing to copy in an examination despite mockery is स्वाभिमान; refusing to apologise after hurting a classmate 'because of my honour' is अहङ्कार. Thus the statement stands: one is inner wealth, the other inner poverty.
questions.explanation: A complete answer defines both terms, cites story and verses, states the tests, and applies them to daily life.

questions.question: 'मानो हि महतां धनम्' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
options: Self-respect indeed is the wealth of the great
Gold indeed is the wealth of the great
Kingdom indeed is the wealth of the great
Fame indeed is the wealth of kings
questions.answer: Self-respect indeed is the wealth of the great
questions.explanation: मानः = self-respect, हि = indeed, महताम् = of the great, धनम् = wealth.

questions.question: In this chapter, the word मानः is used in the sense of —
questions.explanation: मानः here means dignity/self-respect, not anger or negative pride.

questions.question: स्वाभिमानः इति पदं कयोः योगेन निष्पन्नम्? (स्वाभिमानः is formed from which two parts?)
questions.explanation: स्वस्य अभिमानः — rightful honour of one's own self.

questions.question: According to the chapter, why is self-respect called धनम् (wealth)?
options: Because it cannot be stolen — only surrendered
Because it can be exchanged for gold
questions.answer: Because it cannot be stolen — only surrendered
questions.explanation: Gold can be stolen and kingdoms conquered, but dignity is lost only when a person himself gives it up.

questions.question: The chapter presents which word as the counterfeit (perversion) of मानः?
questions.explanation: अहङ्कारः (arrogance) looks like firmness but is rooted in ego, not values.

questions.question: According to the chapter, great people value मान above —
questions.explanation: वरं प्राणपरित्यागो मानभङ्गेन जीवनात् — even life is counted less than unbroken honour.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a mark of true स्वाभिमानः as taught in the chapter?
options: Refusing what is unjust or degrading
Bearing hardship with a calm face
Giving others the same dignity one claims
questions.explanation: Insulting the weak is the mark of अहङ्कार; self-respect honours others.

questions.question: Which Sanskrit word of the chapter means 'honour/dignity won by giving'?
questions.explanation: गौरवं प्राप्यते दानात् — honour is obtained by giving.

questions.question: The chapter says dignity must not harden into stubbornness. On what alone should the धीर stand firm?
questions.explanation: Firmness is dignity only when the issue is justice/values — not every whim of ego.

questions.question: महताम् इति पदस्य कः अर्थः अत्र? (What does महताम् mean in the title?)
questions.explanation: महताम् is षष्ठी (genitive) बहुवचन of महत् — 'of the great'.

questions.question: कथायां नायकस्य किं नाम? (What is the hero's name in the story?)
questions.explanation: Viravarman is the self-respecting chieftain of the hill fort.

questions.question: वीरवर्मा कुत्र नृपतिः आसीत्? (Where was Viravarman king?)
questions.explanation: आसीत् पुरा गिरिदुर्गे वीरवर्मा नाम नृपतिः।

questions.question: बलवतः सम्राजः किं नाम? (What was the powerful emperor's name?)
questions.explanation: Emperor Chandasena conquered the region and sent the offer.

questions.question: What exactly did the emperor demand in return for gold, palace and kingdom?
options: That Viravarman bow in court and accept servitude
That Viravarman marry into his family
questions.answer: That Viravarman bow in court and accept servitude
questions.explanation: शिरः नमयति, दासभावं च स्वीकरोति — bow the head and accept दासभाव.

questions.question: वने वीरवर्मा किम् अखादत्? (What did Viravarman eat in the forest?)
questions.explanation: He ate coarse grass-grain bread and slept on the bare ground.

questions.question: कति वारं सम्राजः दूताः सुवर्णं गृहीत्वा आगच्छन्? (How many times did the emperor's envoys come with gold?)
questions.explanation: Three times they came with more gold; three times he politely refused.

questions.question: After his horse trampled the field, what did Viravarman give the farmer?
questions.explanation: He begged forgiveness and gave his last ring as compensation.

questions.question: कस्य क्षेत्रं वीरवर्मणः अश्वः अमर्दयत्? (Whose field did Viravarman's horse trample?)
questions.explanation: तस्य अश्वः कृषकस्य क्षेत्रम् अमर्दयत्।

questions.question: How does the story end?
options: The emperor returns the kingdom unconditionally and asks for friendship
Viravarman conquers the emperor in battle
Viravarman finally bows and accepts servitude
The emperor exiles Viravarman for ever
questions.answer: The emperor returns the kingdom unconditionally and asks for friendship
questions.explanation: निःशर्तं राज्यं प्रत्यर्पितवान्, मित्रतां च अयाचत — and Viravarman accepted as an equal.

questions.question: When did Viravarman say 'मानः एव महतां धनम्'?
options: While refusing the emperor's offer of wealth for servitude
questions.answer: While refusing the emperor's offer of wealth for servitude
questions.explanation: The line is his answer to the envoy's offer — self-respect alone is the wealth of the great.

questions.question: Why did Viravarman call the offered kingdom 'दास्यम् एव, न राज्यम्' (only servitude, not a kingdom)?
options: Because a kingdom bought by selling self-respect makes its ruler a slave
Because the kingdom offered was too small
Because he feared the emperor's army
Because the palace was far from his home
questions.answer: Because a kingdom bought by selling self-respect makes its ruler a slave
questions.explanation: Once dignity is sold, the 'king' rules only at the master's pleasure — inwardly he is a दास.

questions.question: Which act in the story best proves that Viravarman's firmness was self-respect and NOT arrogance?
options: Begging the farmer's pardon and giving his last ring
Leaving his kingdom for the forest
questions.answer: Begging the farmer's pardon and giving his last ring
questions.explanation: An arrogant man could refuse an emperor; only a self-respecting man can also apologise to a poor farmer.

questions.question: What amazed emperor Chandasena about Viravarman?
options: That a poor man would apologise to a farmer yet not sell his honour for gold
That he survived so long in the forest
That he still had a ring left to give
That his family stayed with him
questions.answer: That a poor man would apologise to a farmer yet not sell his honour for gold
questions.explanation: यः दरिद्रः अपि क्षमां याचते, स्वमानं तु न विक्रीणाति, सः एव सत्यं महान्।

questions.question: What is the central irony (paradox) of the story?
options: By refusing wealth he finally regained wealth, kingdom and fame
By fighting he lost the war
By hoarding gold he became poor
By flattering the emperor he was exiled
questions.answer: By refusing wealth he finally regained wealth, kingdom and fame
questions.explanation: मानेन एव सः धनं राज्यं यशः च पुनः अलभत — dignity proved the better investment.

questions.question: Viravarman's refusal always included 'युष्माकं स्वामिने मम प्रणामाः सन्तु' (my salutations to your master). What does this show?
options: Firmness can be expressed without insult or hatred
He secretly wished to accept the offer
questions.answer: Firmness can be expressed without insult or hatred
questions.explanation: He rejects the condition, not the person — courtesy and firmness coexist in true dignity.

questions.question: What does the detail 'तस्य मुखे शान्तिः आसीत्' (there was peace on his face) during the forest hardship suggest?
options: A clear conscience makes hardship bearable
He had hidden treasure in the forest
He did not understand his poverty
questions.answer: A clear conscience makes hardship bearable
questions.explanation: Outer poverty with inner dignity brings peace; outer riches with inner servitude cannot.

questions.question: Why did Viravarman accept the emperor's friendship at the end, though he had refused his gold before?
options: Friendship was offered between equals, with no condition of servitude
The gold offered this time was greater
He was too weak to refuse again
His family forced him to accept
questions.answer: Friendship was offered between equals, with no condition of servitude
questions.explanation: His objection was never to the emperor but to दासभाव; an unconditional, equal friendship involves no loss of dignity.

questions.question: In the story, दासभावः implies —
options: the inner mentality of servitude, not just outward service
an official post in the court
questions.answer: the inner mentality of servitude, not just outward service
questions.explanation: The emperor demanded not work but submission of the self — which is why it could not be accepted.

questions.question: 'नृपतिः' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: नृपतिः = protector/lord of men, a king.

questions.question: 'दूतः' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: दूतः is the envoy sent by the emperor with the offer.

questions.question: 'सुवर्णम्' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: सुवर्णम् = gold; the emperor offered it thrice.

questions.question: 'प्रासादः' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: प्रासादः = palace, mansion; also seen in प्रासादशिखरस्थः (perched on a palace-top).

questions.question: 'कृषकः' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: कृषकः = one who ploughs, a farmer.

questions.question: 'अङ्गुलीयकम्' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: अङ्गुलीयकम् = finger-ring (from अङ्गुलि, finger).

questions.question: 'क्षमा' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: क्षमां याचितवान् = he begged forgiveness.

questions.question: 'यशः' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: यशः = fame; Viravarman regained धनं राज्यं यशः च.

questions.question: 'निराकरोत्' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: निराकरोत् = he refused/rejected (the envoys' offer), politely.

questions.question: 'शीर्यते' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: Used of the palace (प्रासादः शीर्यते) and the flower-cluster withering in the forest (शीर्यते वन एव वा).

questions.question: 'धीराः' (in निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणाः...) means —
questions.explanation: धीराः are those of firm mind who never leave the just path.

questions.question: 'मनस्वी' (verse: द्वयी वृत्तिर्मनस्विनः) means —
questions.explanation: मनस्वी = one with (noble) mind — the self-respecting person compared to a flower-cluster.

questions.question: 'निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु...' — this verse is from which work?
questions.explanation: It is a famous stanza of Bhartrhari's Nitishataka on the steadfastness of the धीर.

questions.question: 'निन्दन्तु' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: निन्दन्तु (लोट्) = let them censure/blame; स्तुवन्तु = let them praise.

questions.question: In Bhartrhari's verse, what may Lakshmi (लक्ष्मीः) do while the धीराः remain unmoved?
options: Come or go as she pleases
questions.answer: Come or go as she pleases
questions.explanation: लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् — fortune may enter or depart at will.

questions.question: According to कुसुमस्तबकस्येव..., what are the only two courses (द्वयी वृत्तिः) of the self-respecting person?
options: To rest on the world's head, or wither in the forest
To gain wealth, or lose wealth
To rule a kingdom, or serve a king
To speak sweetly, or stay silent
questions.answer: To rest on the world's head, or wither in the forest
questions.explanation: मूर्ध्नि वा सर्वलोकस्य शीर्यते वन एव वा — full honour or dignified obscurity, never trampling.

questions.question: 'कुसुमस्तबकः' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: कुसुमानां स्तबकः — a bunch/cluster of flowers, the simile for the मनस्वी.

questions.question: According to 'वरं प्राणपरित्यागो...', what is better than living with broken honour?
questions.explanation: वरं प्राणपरित्यागो मानभङ्गेन जीवनात् — death is preferred to a life of humiliation.

questions.question: प्राणत्यागे क्षणं दुःखम् — मानभङ्गे तु कदा दुःखम्?
questions.explanation: Broken honour brings pain repeatedly, every day — the वीप्सा दिने दिने.

questions.question: गुणैरुत्तमतां याति — कैः उत्तमतां याति जनः? (By what does one attain greatness?)
questions.explanation: Greatness comes from virtues, not from occupying a high seat.

questions.question: प्रासादशिखरस्थोऽपि काकः किं गरुडायते — what does this line teach?
options: A high position without merit gives no real greatness
Crows can learn to fly like Garuda
Palaces should be kept free of birds
questions.answer: A high position without merit gives no real greatness
questions.explanation: Even perched on a palace-top, a crow does not become Garuda — honour rests on worth, not seat.

questions.question: गौरवं प्राप्यते ____ — केन गौरवं प्राप्यते? (By what is honour obtained, in verse 5?)
questions.explanation: गौरवं प्राप्यते दानात् न तु वित्तस्य सञ्चयात्।

questions.question: In verse 5, why do the clouds (पयोदाः) stand high while the oceans (पयोधयः) lie below?
options: Clouds give water while oceans hoard it
Oceans are afraid of the sky
questions.answer: Clouds give water while oceans hoard it
questions.explanation: The giver rises, the hoarder sinks — nature's image of honour through generosity.

questions.question: 'यथेष्टम्' इत्यस्य कः अर्थः?
questions.explanation: यथेष्टम् (अव्ययीभाव) = according to wish — fortune may go 'as she pleases'.

questions.question: 'मानो हि' इत्यस्य सन्धि-विच्छेदः कः?
questions.explanation: The visarga of मानः becomes ओ before the soft consonant ह् — विसर्ग-सन्धि.

questions.question: 'मानो हि' — अत्र कः सन्धिः?
questions.explanation: ः + soft consonant → ओ; this is a visarga sandhi.

questions.question: 'अद्यैव' इत्यस्य सन्धि-विच्छेदः कः?
questions.explanation: अ + ए = ऐ, वृद्धि-सन्धि: अद्य + एव = अद्यैव ('this very day').

questions.question: 'नास्ति' इत्यस्य सन्धि-विच्छेदः कः?
questions.explanation: अ + अ = आ (दीर्घ-सन्धि): न + अस्ति = नास्ति.

questions.question: 'प्राणपरित्यागः' — अस्य कः समासः?
questions.explanation: प्राणानां परित्यागः — 'abandonment OF life', a genitive tatpurusha.

questions.question: 'नीतिनिपुणः' इत्यस्य कः विग्रहः?
questions.explanation: 'Skilled IN ethics' — सप्तमी-तत्पुरुष with locative sense.

questions.question: 'महताम्' (मानो हि महतां धनम्) — का विभक्तिः, किं वचनम्?
questions.explanation: महताम् = 'of the great (ones)' — genitive plural of महत्.

questions.question: 'गुणैः' (गुणैरुत्तमतां याति) — का विभक्तिः?
questions.explanation: गुणैः = 'BY virtues' — instrumental (तृतीया) plural.

questions.question: 'वने' (शीर्यते वन एव वा) — का विभक्तिः?
questions.explanation: वने = 'in the forest' — locative (सप्तमी) singular.

questions.question: 'जीवनात्' (वरं प्राणपरित्यागो मानभङ्गेन जीवनात्) — का विभक्तिः, केन प्रयोजनेन?
options: पञ्चमी — comparison with वरम् ('better THAN living')
questions.answer: पञ्चमी — comparison with वरम् ('better THAN living')
questions.explanation: With वरम् the thing surpassed takes the ablative (पञ्चमी) — 'better than a life with broken honour'.

questions.question: 'निन्दन्तु', 'स्तुवन्तु', 'अस्तु' — एतेषु कः लकारः?
questions.explanation: All are imperatives ('let them blame/praise, let it be') — लोट् लकार.

questions.question: 'याति' (गुणैरुत्तमतां याति) — कः लकारः?
questions.explanation: याति = 'attains/goes' — simple present, लट् लकार.

questions.question: 'दास्यामि' (अहं तस्मै राज्यं दास्यामि) — कः लकारः?
questions.explanation: दास्यामि = 'I SHALL give' — simple future, लृट् लकार.

questions.question: According to the chapter, the root difference between स्वाभिमानः and अहङ्कारः is —
options: Self-respect is rooted in values; arrogance is rooted in comparison with others
Self-respect belongs to kings; arrogance to commoners
Self-respect is loud; arrogance is quiet
questions.answer: Self-respect is rooted in values; arrogance is rooted in comparison with others
questions.explanation: स्वाभिमान refuses only the unjust and honours others; अहङ्कार wants to stand above others.

questions.question: Which behaviour is a sign of अहङ्कारः rather than मानः?
options: Refusing to apologise even when clearly in the wrong
Refusing to cheat in an examination
Bearing poverty with a calm face
questions.answer: Refusing to apologise even when clearly in the wrong
questions.explanation: The test of the chapter: self-respect can say 'I was wrong'; arrogance cannot.

questions.question: A student refuses to copy answers in an examination although friends mock him. This is —
options: स्वाभिमानः — firmness on the just path
questions.answer: स्वाभिमानः — firmness on the just path
questions.explanation: He refuses something degrading/unjust despite social pressure — dignity, not ego.

questions.question: A boy insults a poor classmate saying 'sitting with him is beneath my honour'. The chapter would call this —
options: अहङ्कारः — false honour that insults the weak
questions.answer: अहङ्कारः — false honour that insults the weak
questions.explanation: True मान gives every person the same dignity it claims; contempt for the weak is arrogance.

questions.question: The crow perched on the palace tower (verse 4) is the chapter's image of —
questions.explanation: A high seat cannot supply the worth that only गुण (virtue) gives.

questions.question: When does firm refusal STOP being dignity and become ego, according to the chapter's balance of wisdom?
options: When it hardens into stubbornness over trifles instead of matters of justice
When it costs the person wealth
questions.answer: When it hardens into stubbornness over trifles instead of matters of justice
questions.explanation: The धीर stands firm on the न्याय्य पथ — the just path — not on every whim of ego.

questions.question: Choose the correct English translation of: मानः एव महतां धनम्।
options: Self-respect alone is the wealth of the great
Wealth alone brings self-respect to the great
The great alone deserve wealth and respect
Respect the wealth of great people
questions.answer: Self-respect alone is the wealth of the great
questions.explanation: एव = alone/indeed; महताम् = of the great; धनम् = wealth.

questions.question: Choose the correct Sanskrit for: 'The steadfast do not abandon the path of justice.'
questions.explanation: Plural subject धीराः, object न्याय्यं पथम् (द्वितीया), verb न त्यजन्ति.

questions.question: 'सः राज्यं त्यक्त्वा वनम् अगच्छत्।' — Choose the correct translation.
options: Having abandoned the kingdom, he went to the forest
He abandoned the forest and went to the kingdom
He will leave the kingdom for the forest
He rules the kingdom from the forest
questions.answer: Having abandoned the kingdom, he went to the forest
questions.explanation: त्यक्त्वा is the gerund 'having abandoned'; अगच्छत् is past 'went'.

questions.question: Choose the correct Sanskrit for: 'Honour is obtained by giving.'
questions.explanation: दानेन (तृतीया, 'by giving') + गौरवम् (subject of passive) + लभ्यते ('is obtained').

questions.question: True or False: In this chapter the word मानः means arrogance and is condemned as a vice.
questions.explanation: मानः here means self-respect (आत्मगौरवम्), praised as the wealth of the great; the vice is अहङ्कारः.

questions.question: True or False: Viravarman went to the forest alone, leaving his family in the palace.
questions.explanation: सपरिवारः वनम् अगच्छत् — he went to the forest together with his family.

questions.question: True or False: In the end, emperor Chandasena himself came to the forest and returned Viravarman's kingdom without any condition.
questions.explanation: सः स्वयं वनम् अगच्छत्, निःशर्तं तस्य राज्यं प्रत्यर्पितवान् — unconditionally.

questions.question: True or False: The story shows that self-respect and courtesy can live together in the same person.
questions.explanation: Viravarman refuses an emperor firmly yet politely, and apologises to a farmer — firmness with courtesy.

questions.question: True or False: The word सुवर्णम् means 'silver'.
questions.explanation: सुवर्णम् means gold; silver is रजतम्.

questions.question: True or False: The verse निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु is attributed to Bhartrhari's नीतिशतकम्.
questions.explanation: It is one of the most famous stanzas of the Nitishataka, on the steadfast धीर.

questions.question: True or False: According to वरं प्राणपरित्यागो..., the pain of broken honour lasts only a moment.
questions.explanation: It is the pain of death that lasts a moment; broken honour pains दिने दिने — day after day.

questions.question: True or False: मानो हि is formed from मानः + हि by विसर्ग-सन्धि.
questions.explanation: Before the soft consonant ह्, the visarga of मानः becomes ओ.

questions.question: True or False: According to the chapter, insulting weaker people is sometimes a necessary part of protecting one's स्वाभिमान.
questions.explanation: Insulting the weak is the mark of अहङ्कार; true self-respect gives others the dignity it claims for itself.

questions.question: True or False: 'धीराः पदं न प्रविचलन्ति' may be translated as 'the steadfast do not swerve even a step'.
questions.explanation: पदम् = a step; प्रविचलन्ति = swerve/deviate; न = not.

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: मानो हि महतां ____ ।
questions.explanation: The chapter's title maxim: self-respect indeed is the WEALTH (धनम्) of the great.

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: स्व + अभिमानः = ____ ।
questions.explanation: स्व + अभिमानः joins by दीर्घ-सन्धि (अ + अ = आ) to give स्वाभिमानः, self-respect.

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: आसीत् पुरा गिरिदुर्गे ____ नाम नृपतिः।
questions.explanation: The story's opening names the hero — Viravarman, king in the hill fort.

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: ____ नाम बलवान् सम्राट् तं देशम् अजयत्।
questions.explanation: Emperor Chandasena conquered the region.

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: सः राज्यं त्यक्त्वा सपरिवारः ____ अगच्छत्।
questions.explanation: He abandoned the kingdom and went to the FOREST (वनम्) with his family.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the English meaning: नृपतिः = ____ .
questions.explanation: नृपतिः (lord of men) = king.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the English meaning: क्षमा = ____ .
questions.explanation: क्षमा = forgiveness/pardon; Viravarman begged it of the farmer (क्षमां याचितवान्).

questions.question: श्लोकं पूरयत: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा ____ ।
questions.explanation: Let them blame or PRAISE (स्तुवन्तु) — the steadfast remain unmoved.

questions.question: श्लोकं पूरयत: वरं प्राणपरित्यागो ____ जीवनात्।
questions.explanation: Better to give up life than to live WITH BROKEN HONOUR (मानभङ्गेन).

questions.question: श्लोकं पूरयत: गुणैः ____ याति नोच्चैरासनसंस्थितः।
questions.explanation: By virtues one attains GREATNESS (उत्तमताम्), not by a high seat.

questions.question: सन्धिं कुरुत: मानः + हि = ____ ।
questions.explanation: विसर्ग-सन्धि: ः → ओ before the soft consonant ह्.

questions.question: सन्धिं कुरुत: अद्य + एव = ____ ।
questions.explanation: वृद्धि-सन्धि: अ + ए = ऐ, giving अद्यैव ('this very day').

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: 'महताम्' इति पदे ____ विभक्तिः अस्ति। (Name the vibhakti.)
questions.explanation: महताम् = 'of the great' — genitive (षष्ठी) plural of महत्.

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: 'निन्दन्तु' इति क्रियापदे ____ लकारः अस्ति। (Name the lakara.)
questions.explanation: निन्दन्तु 'let them blame' is an imperative — लोट् लकार.

questions.question: रिक्तस्थानं पूरयत: स्वाभिमानी अन्यान् सम्मानयति, ____ तु अन्यान् अपमानयति। (Which quality insults others?)
questions.explanation: The self-respecting person honours others; the ARROGANT (अहङ्कारी) insults them.

questions.question: Explain the maxim मानो हि महतां धनम् in two or three sentences.
questions.answer: The maxim means 'self-respect indeed is the wealth of the great'. Gold and kingdoms can be seized by others, but dignity (आत्मगौरवम्) can only be surrendered by oneself; therefore noble people treasure it as their real wealth. Whoever keeps it is rich even in poverty; whoever sells it is poor even on a throne.
questions.explanation: Definition of मानः as self-respect plus the reason it is called imperishable wealth.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say that मान can only be surrendered, never stolen? What follows from this for the great?
questions.answer: Thieves can steal gold and armies can seize kingdoms, but no outside force can take away a person's self-respect — it is lost only when the person himself agrees to a degrading bargain. Therefore the great guard it as the one possession fully in their own power, and refuse any price offered for it, as Viravarman refused the emperor's gold.
questions.explanation: The inalienability of dignity is the ground of the maxim.

questions.question: धनम् (wealth) and मानः (self-respect) — compare the two as 'possessions' using three differences given in the chapter.
questions.answer: 1) Wealth perishes (धनं नश्यति) and passes from hand to hand; self-respect endures as long as its owner wills. 2) Wealth can be stolen or conquered; self-respect can only be surrendered. 3) Wealth without dignity gives no peace (a gilded servitude), while dignity without wealth still leaves peace on the face, as in Viravarman's forest life. Hence मान is the truer wealth.
questions.explanation: Perishability, alienability, and relation to inner peace distinguish the two.

questions.question: What offer did emperor Chandasena send to Viravarman, and on what condition?
questions.answer: He offered gold (सुवर्णम्), a palace (प्रासादः) and a vast kingdom (विशालं राज्यम्) — on condition that Viravarman come to the imperial court, bow his head (शिरः नमयति) and accept servitude (दासभावं स्वीकरोति).
questions.explanation: The offer and its degrading condition set up the story's central choice.

questions.question: Describe Viravarman's life in the forest in two or three sentences.
questions.answer: His life was hard: he ate bread made of wild grass-grain (तृणधान्यस्य रोटिका) and slept on the bare ground (भूमौ शेते स्म). Yet there was peace on his face, because his conscience was clear. Even when envoys came thrice with more gold, he refused politely each time.
questions.explanation: Hardship borne with calm — outer poverty, inner dignity.

questions.question: How does the story of Viravarman end? Mention all three things he regained.
questions.answer: Amazed by the man who apologised to a farmer yet would not sell his honour for gold, emperor Chandasena himself came to the forest, returned the kingdom unconditionally (निःशर्तम्) and asked for friendship. Viravarman accepted the friendship as an equal (समभावेन). Thus through self-respect alone he regained wealth (धनम्), kingdom (राज्यम्) and fame (यशः).
questions.explanation: एवं मानेन एव सः धनं राज्यं यशः च पुनः अलभत।

questions.question: Some would call Viravarman's refusal foolishness — he gave up a real kingdom for a principle. Argue, from the story, why it was dignity and not foolishness.
questions.answer: The kingdom offered was not real power but gilded servitude: it could be enjoyed only at the emperor's pleasure, after publicly surrendering his self (दासभावः). Viravarman judged that what perishes (gold, palace) should not be bought with what need never perish (dignity). Events proved him right: his unsold honour moved the emperor to return everything unconditionally, so he ended with kingdom, wealth, fame — and his मान intact. A fool trades the permanent for the perishable; Viravarman did the opposite.
questions.explanation: The refusal weighed perishable goods against imperishable dignity, and the ending vindicates the choice.

questions.question: Mention two acts of Viravarman that show humility, and state what they prove about his character.
questions.answer: He bowed to his aged teacher and spoke respectfully to the potter and the farmer; and when his horse trampled a farmer's field he himself begged forgiveness and gave his last ring. These prove that his firmness before the emperor was self-respect, not arrogance — he gave others the same dignity he claimed for himself.
questions.explanation: Humility toward the humble is the story's test separating मान from अहङ्कार.

questions.question: Why is it significant that Viravarman's refusals were always courteous ('युष्माकं स्वामिने मम प्रणामाः सन्तु')? What would an insulting refusal have shown instead?
questions.answer: The courteous refusal shows he rejected the condition (servitude), not the person of the emperor — his stand was on principle, free of hatred or wounded vanity. An insulting refusal would have been ego answering ego: it would prove he was defending his pride against a rival, not his dignity against injustice, and would make him अहङ्कारी rather than स्वाभिमानी. Courtesy in firmness is exactly what finally won the emperor's heart.
questions.explanation: Manner reveals motive: politeness marks principle; insult marks ego.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of: दासभावः, तृणधान्यम्, सविनयम्, निःशर्तम्, समभावेन.
questions.answer: दासभावः = attitude/condition of servitude; तृणधान्यम् = wild grass-grain; सविनयम् = politely, with humility; निःशर्तम् = unconditionally; समभावेन = with equanimity, as an equal.
questions.explanation: All five occur at turning points of the story.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of these words from the verses: धीराः, मनस्वी, मानभङ्गः, गरुडायते, पयोदाः.
questions.answer: धीराः = the steadfast/resolute; मनस्वी = a high-minded, self-respecting person; मानभङ्गः = breaking of honour; गरुडायते = acts like/becomes Garuda; पयोदाः = clouds (givers of water).
questions.explanation: Key vocabulary of the five niti verses.

questions.question: Write the अन्वय of निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु... and give its meaning in two sentences.
questions.answer: अन्वय: नीतिनिपुणाः निन्दन्तु यदि वा स्तुवन्तु, लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु वा यथेष्टं गच्छतु, मरणम् अद्य एव अस्तु युगान्तरे वा — धीराः न्याय्यात् पथः पदं न प्रविचलन्ति। Meaning: Let experts blame or praise, let fortune come or go at her pleasure, let death come today or after an age. The steadfast never swerve even one step from the path of justice.
questions.explanation: Three concessions (critics, fortune, death) against one refusal — leaving the just path.

questions.question: Explain the simile of the flower-cluster (कुसुमस्तबकः) for the self-respecting person.
questions.answer: A flower-cluster has only two fates: to be worn on the head with honour, or to wither unseen in the forest — it is never left half-trampled. Likewise the मनस्वी lives either with full honour or in dignified obscurity; he accepts hardship but never humiliation.
questions.explanation: द्वयी वृत्तिः — two courses only, no middle state of degradation.

questions.question: Explain why the verse says a moment's pain of death is preferable to broken honour.
questions.answer: In giving up life the pain is felt once, for a moment (प्राणत्यागे क्षणं दुःखम्); but one who lives on with broken honour tastes humiliation afresh every single day (मानभङ्गे दिने दिने). The verse weighs a single pang against an endless series of pangs, and finds dishonoured life the heavier suffering.
questions.explanation: The arithmetic of suffering: one moment versus every day.

questions.question: Explain the imagery of गौरवं प्राप्यते दानात्... — how do the clouds and the oceans teach the source of honour?
questions.answer: The verse says honour comes from giving, not from hoarding wealth. Its proof is from nature: the clouds (पयोदाः), which give away their water as rain, occupy the high place in the sky; the oceans (पयोधयः), which hold and hoard vast waters, lie below. Height of position follows generosity, not accumulation — so a person who gives earns गौरव, while a hoarder, however rich, stays 'low'.
questions.explanation: पयोद = water-giver stands high; पयोधि = water-holder lies low — giving elevates.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद and name the sandhi: (a) मानो हि (b) अद्यैव.
questions.answer: (a) मानो हि = मानः + हि — विसर्ग-सन्धिः (ः becomes ओ before the soft consonant ह्). (b) अद्यैव = अद्य + एव — वृद्धि-सन्धिः (अ + ए = ऐ).
questions.explanation: The title itself and a phrase of verse 1 supply the two examples.

questions.question: Give the विग्रह and name the समास: (a) मानभङ्गः (b) नीतिनिपुणः (c) यथेष्टम्.
questions.answer: (a) मानभङ्गः = मानस्य भङ्गः — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः ('breaking OF honour'). (b) नीतिनिपुणः = नीतिषु निपुणः — सप्तमी-तत्पुरुषः ('skilled IN ethics'). (c) यथेष्टम् = इष्टम् अनतिक्रम्य — अव्ययीभावः ('according to wish').
questions.explanation: Two tatpurushas with different case-senses plus one avyayibhava.

questions.question: Identify विभक्ति or लकार as asked: (a) महताम् — vibhakti and vachana; (b) जीवनात् — vibhakti and its special use here; (c) दास्यामि — lakara.
questions.answer: (a) महताम् — षष्ठी विभक्तिः, बहुवचनम् ('of the great'). (b) जीवनात् — पञ्चमी विभक्तिः; with वरम् it is the ablative of comparison, 'better THAN living (with broken honour)'. (c) दास्यामि — लृट् लकारः (simple future, 'I shall give').
questions.explanation: Three flagship grammar forms of the chapter.

questions.question: State three tests given in the chapter for telling स्वाभिमान from अहङ्कार, and apply any one of them to Viravarman.
questions.answer: Tests: (1) Self-respect can apologise and admit a fault; arrogance cannot. (2) Self-respect honours others — even the weak; arrogance insults them. (3) Self-respect bears hardship calmly; arrogance bears no slight, however small. Applying test (1): Viravarman, though a king, himself begged a farmer's pardon when his horse ruined the field — proof that his firmness before the emperor was dignity, not ego.
questions.explanation: The apology test, the respect test, and the calm-endurance test.

questions.question: When can insistence on 'my honour' actually become अहङ्कार? Give one everyday example and the chapter's criterion for judging it.
questions.answer: Insistence on honour becomes अहङ्कार when the issue is not justice or values but mere ego — e.g. a student who refuses to apologise to a classmate he hurt 'because apologising is beneath me', or one who sulks for days over not being greeted first. The chapter's criterion: the धीर stands firm only on the न्याय्य पथ (the just path); firmness over trifles, or firmness that requires insulting others, is ego wearing the mask of dignity.
questions.explanation: The just-path criterion separates principled firmness from stubborn vanity.

questions.question: Translate into simple English: धनं नश्यति, प्रासादः शीर्यते, राज्यं हस्तात् हस्तं गच्छति। मानः एव महतां धनम्।
questions.answer: Wealth perishes, the palace crumbles, a kingdom passes from hand to hand. Self-respect alone is the wealth of the great.
questions.explanation: Viravarman's reply to the envoy — the story's statement of the title maxim.

questions.question: Compose three simple Sanskrit sentences (in Devanagari) on स्वाभिमान, and give their English meanings.
questions.answer: 1. मानः महतां धनम् अस्ति। (Self-respect is the wealth of the great.) 2. स्वाभिमानी जनः असत्यं न वदति। (A self-respecting person does not speak untruth.) 3. सः कष्टं सहते, किन्तु मानं न त्यजति। (He endures hardship, but does not abandon his self-respect.)
questions.explanation: Model answer; any grammatically correct sentences on the theme are acceptable.

questions.question: 'मानो हि महतां धनम्' — explain the meaning and significance of this maxim, illustrating it from the story of Viravarman and from at least two niti verses of the chapter.
questions.answer: The maxim declares self-respect (मानः, आत्मगौरवम्) to be the true wealth of the great. Ordinary wealth is perishable and alienable — it can be stolen, conquered, or lost; dignity is imperishable and inalienable — it is lost only if its owner sells it. The story illustrates this: Viravarman refuses gold, palace and kingdom because their price is दासभावः, saying 'a kingdom bought by selling self-respect is only servitude'. In the forest he is materially poor but inwardly rich — peace stays on his face — and finally his unsold dignity wins back wealth, kingdom and fame, showing that मान even 'earns' like wealth. The verses deepen the point: Bhartrhari's धीराः treat fortune's coming and going as trifles beside the just path (निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणाः...); the maxim वरं प्राणपरित्यागो मानभङ्गेन जीवनात् prices honour above life itself; and गौरवं प्राप्यते दानात् shows honour is earned by virtue and giving, not by hoarding. Together they teach that character, not coin, is the currency of greatness.
questions.explanation: Definition, contrast with perishable wealth, story evidence, and at least two verses woven together.

questions.question: Write a character sketch of Viravarman, bringing out at least four qualities with one incident from the story for each.
questions.answer: 1) Self-respecting (स्वाभिमानी): he refuses an empire offered at the price of bowing into servitude — 'मानः एव महतां धनम्'. 2) Steadfast (धीरः): three times envoys return with more gold; three times his answer is unchanged, proving his refusal was principle, not mood. 3) Humble and courteous (विनयी): he bows to his aged teacher, speaks respectfully to potter and farmer, and even his refusals carry salutations to the emperor — firmness without insult. 4) Just and responsible (न्यायपरः): when his horse tramples a farmer's field, he himself begs forgiveness and gives his last ring in compensation, though he is now poor. 5) Even-minded (समभावः): he bears forest hardship with peace on his face, and at the end accepts the emperor's friendship without triumph or bitterness, as an equal. In him the chapter's ideal is complete: dignity before the mighty, gentleness before the humble.
questions.explanation: Quality-plus-incident structure; four or more traits required.

questions.question: Analyse the transformation of emperor Chandasena in the story. What did he learn about greatness, and how does his final act prove the maxim of the chapter?
questions.answer: Chandasena begins believing that everything has a price: having conquered the land, he assumes gold, palace and kingdom can buy even a man's dignity. Viravarman's three refusals puzzle him; but the report of the farmer episode transforms him — here is a man now poor who begs pardon of a peasant, yet will not sell his honour for imperial gold. Chandasena realises that greatness lies not in power or treasury but in character: 'यः दरिद्रः अपि क्षमां याचते, स्वमानं तु न विक्रीणाति, सः एव सत्यं महान्'. His final act — going himself to the forest, returning the kingdom unconditionally, and asking (not commanding) friendship — proves the maxim: the emperor with all his wealth comes as a suitor to the man whose only wealth was मान. Dignity, which could not be bought, ends by commanding even the buyer. The conqueror of lands is conquered by self-respect.
questions.explanation: From 'everything has a price' to honouring the priceless; the ending inverts buyer and seller.

questions.question: Explain Bhartrhari's verse निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु... fully: give its अन्वय, word meanings of the key terms, its central idea, and its relevance for a student today.
questions.answer: अन्वय: नीतिनिपुणाः निन्दन्तु यदि वा स्तुवन्तु; लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु वा यथेष्टं गच्छतु; मरणम् अद्य एव अस्तु युगान्तरे वा — धीराः न्याय्यात् पथः पदं न प्रविचलन्ति। Key words: नीतिनिपुणाः = experts in policy/ethics; निन्दन्तु/स्तुवन्तु = let them blame/praise (लोट्); लक्ष्मीः = fortune; यथेष्टम् = as she pleases; युगान्तरे = after an age; धीराः = the steadfast; प्रविचलन्ति = swerve. Central idea: the verse lists the three great pressures that bend ordinary people — public opinion (praise/blame), material fortune (Lakshmi's coming and going), and fear of death — and declares that the steadfast yield to none of them: they will not leave the just path by even one step (पदम्). Relevance today: a student faces the same three pressures — peer opinion and mockery, temptation of easy gain (copying, shortcuts), and fear of loss or failure. The verse teaches that self-respect means anchoring conduct in what is right, not in applause, profit or fear; examinations of character, like examinations of Sanskrit, are passed by steadiness.
questions.explanation: Anvaya, shabdartha, the three pressures versus one refusal, and a modern application.

questions.question: From the chapter, write a grammar note covering: (a) two सन्धि examples with their names and splits; (b) two समास examples with विग्रह and names; (c) two विभक्ति identifications; (d) two लकार identifications.
questions.answer: (a) सन्धि: मानो हि = मानः + हि — विसर्ग-सन्धिः (visarga → ओ before soft ह्); अद्यैव = अद्य + एव — वृद्धि-सन्धिः (अ + ए = ऐ). (Also नास्ति = न + अस्ति, दीर्घ.) (b) समास: प्राणपरित्यागः = प्राणानां परित्यागः — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः; नीतिनिपुणः = नीतिषु निपुणः — सप्तमी-तत्पुरुषः. (Also यथेष्टम् — अव्ययीभावः.) (c) विभक्ति: महताम् (महत्) — षष्ठी बहुवचनम्, 'of the great', as in the title; जीवनात् — पञ्चमी एकवचनम्, ablative of comparison with वरम्, 'better than living'. (Also गुणैः — तृतीया, 'by virtues'; दिने दिने — सप्तमी with repetition.) (d) लकार: निन्दन्तु, स्तुवन्तु, अस्तु — लोट् (imperative 'let them...'); दास्यामि — लृट् (future 'I shall give'); याति — लट् (present); अगच्छत् — लङ् (past).
questions.explanation: A complete grammar harvest of the chapter across sandhi, samasa, vibhakti and lakara.

questions.question: 'स्वाभिमानः and अहङ्कारः both refuse to bend — yet one is a virtue and the other a vice.' Discuss this statement with the chapter's tests, one example from the story, and two examples from modern life.
questions.answer: Both look alike from outside: a straight back, a firm 'no'. The difference is inside. स्वाभिमान is rooted in values — it refuses only what is unjust or degrading, and it grants every other person the same dignity it claims; अहङ्कार is rooted in comparison — it wants to stand above others, demands honour it has not earned, and treats every disagreement as an insult. The chapter's tests: self-respect can apologise ('I was wrong'); arrogance cannot. Self-respect bears hardship calmly; arrogance bears no slight. Self-respect stands firm only on the just path; arrogance is firm everywhere. Story example: the same Viravarman who refuses an emperor bows to his teacher and begs a farmer's pardon — the refusal and the apology together certify his dignity. Modern examples: (1) An employee politely declines to falsify accounts though threatened with dismissal — self-respect: the ground is justice, the manner courteous. (2) A student refuses to say sorry after breaking a classmate's project, calling apology 'humiliation' — arrogance: the ground is ego, and another's dignity is trampled. Thus the same outward firmness is virtue when it guards values and vice when it guards vanity.
questions.explanation: Same posture, different root: values versus ego; tested by apology, treatment of the weak, and the just-path criterion.

questions.question: The verse says 'better death than broken honour' (वरं प्राणपरित्यागो...). Is such an extreme ideal wise guidance for ordinary life? Evaluate both sides using the chapter's own balance of wisdom.
questions.answer: For the ideal: the verse dramatises a true scale of values. It teaches that some things must never be sold — conscience, dignity, justice — and that a life purchased by daily humiliation is a heavier suffering than a moment's pain (मानभङ्गे दिने दिने). History's noblest figures, like Viravarman in our story, drew strength from exactly this absoluteness; a principle with a price-tag is no principle. Against a literal reading: the chapter itself supplies the balance. The धीर stands firm on the न्याय्य पथ — matters of justice and values — not on every scratch to the ego; dignity that hardens into touchiness over trifles is अहङ्कार, not मान. Moreover Viravarman's own model is not death but dignified endurance: he chooses hardship, courtesy and patience, and lives to see honour restored. The wise conclusion: read the verse as a measure of worth, not a literal command — be ready to lose comfort, wealth, position, anything perishable, rather than sell self-respect; but meet insults from others with the flower-cluster's calm, for another's rudeness cannot break the honour that only we ourselves can surrender.
questions.explanation: A balanced evaluation: the verse as value-scale versus literalism; the just-path and endurance model resolve it.

questions.question: Compose a short Sanskrit paragraph of five simple sentences (in Devanagari) titled 'स्वाभिमानस्य महत्त्वम्', and give an English translation of your paragraph.
questions.answer: स्वाभिमानस्य महत्त्वम् — मानः एव महतां धनम् अस्ति। धनं नश्यति, किन्तु मानः न नश्यति। स्वाभिमानी जनः अन्यायं कदापि न स्वीकरोति। सः अन्यान् अपि सम्मानयति, अहङ्कारं च त्यजति। अतः वयं सर्वदा स्वाभिमानेन जीवेम। English: Self-respect alone is the wealth of the great. Wealth perishes, but self-respect does not perish. A self-respecting person never accepts injustice. He honours others too, and gives up arrogance. Therefore let us always live with self-respect. (Model answer — any grammatically sound paragraph on the theme is acceptable.)
questions.explanation: Five sentences using chapter vocabulary; जीवेम is विधिलिङ् 'let us live'.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: सः दूतं प्रेषितवान् — 'यदि वीरवर्मा मम सभायाम् आगत्य शिरः नमयति, दासभावं च स्वीकरोति, तर्हि अहं तस्मै सुवर्णं प्रासादं विशालं राज्यं च दास्यामि' इति। (a) Who sent this message and through whom? (b) List the three things offered. (c) List the two conditions demanded. (d) Give the meaning of दास्यामि.
questions.answer: (a) Emperor Chandasena sent the message through a दूत (envoy/messenger). (b) He offered gold (सुवर्णम्), a palace (प्रासादम्) and a vast kingdom (विशालं राज्यम्). (c) The conditions: Viravarman must come to the imperial court and bow his head (शिरः नमयति), and must accept servitude (दासभावं स्वीकरोति). (d) दास्यामि = 'I shall give' (future, लृट् लकार).
questions.explanation: Comprehension of the offer-passage: sender, gifts, conditions, and the future-tense verb.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: वने तस्य जीवनं कठिनम् आसीत्। सः तृणधान्यस्य रोटिकां खादति स्म, भूमौ शेते स्म। तथापि तस्य मुखे शान्तिः आसीत्। (a) Where does this scene take place? (b) Mention the two hardships described. (c) What was surprising despite the hardships? (d) What does तथापि mean?
questions.answer: (a) In the forest (वने), after Viravarman abandoned his kingdom. (b) He ate bread made of wild grass-grain (तृणधान्यस्य रोटिका) and slept on the bare ground (भूमौ). (c) Despite this, there was peace (शान्तिः) on his face — the calm of a clear conscience and unsold dignity. (d) तथापि = 'even so, nevertheless'.
questions.explanation: The hardship-passage shows outer poverty with inner peace.

questions.question: Read and answer: वीरवर्मा अवदत् — 'धनं नश्यति, प्रासादः शीर्यते, राज्यं हस्तात् हस्तं गच्छति। मानः एव महतां धनम्। स्वाभिमानं विक्रीय लब्धं राज्यं दास्यम् एव भवति, न राज्यम्।' (a) What three examples of perishable things does he give? (b) What single thing does he set against them? (c) Explain the logic of his last sentence. (d) What does विक्रीय mean?
questions.answer: (a) Wealth perishes (धनं नश्यति), palaces crumble (प्रासादः शीर्यते), kingdoms pass from hand to hand (राज्यं हस्तात् हस्तं गच्छति). (b) Against all three he sets मानः — self-respect, the one imperishable wealth of the great. (c) Logic: a kingdom is meant to make one a master; but if it is obtained by selling one's self-respect, its 'king' remains inwardly a slave of the giver — so what is gained is in truth servitude (दास्यम्), not kingship. The means poison the end. (d) विक्रीय = 'having sold' (gerund of वि + क्री).
questions.explanation: The refusal-speech: perishables versus मान, and the self-defeating bargain of bought kingship.

questions.question: Read and answer: त्रिवारं सम्राजः दूताः अधिकं सुवर्णं गृहीत्वा आगच्छन्, त्रिवारं च सः सविनयम् एव निराकरोत् — 'भोः, युष्माकं स्वामिने मम प्रणामाः सन्तु। किन्तु मम उत्तरं तदेव अस्ति' इति। (a) What did the envoys bring each time, and how often did they come? (b) In what manner did Viravarman refuse? (c) What is the significance of sending प्रणामाः to the emperor while refusing him? (d) What does 'मम उत्तरं तदेव अस्ति' reveal about his character?
questions.answer: (a) They came three times (त्रिवारम्), each time bringing more gold (अधिकं सुवर्णम्). (b) He refused politely, with humility (सविनयम्) — never with anger or insult. (c) Sending salutations shows he bore no hatred: he rejected the degrading condition, not the emperor as a person — his stand was principle, not pride or enmity. (d) 'My answer is the same' reveals steadfastness (धैर्यम्): his refusal did not depend on the size of the offer, so raising the price could not change it — the mark of a principle, which has no price.
questions.explanation: Escalating temptation meets constant, courteous refusal — firmness rooted in values.

questions.question: Read and answer: चण्डसेनः चिन्तयित्वा स्वयं वनम् अगच्छत्, निःशर्तं तस्य राज्यं प्रत्यर्पितवान्, मित्रतां च अयाचत। वीरवर्मा समभावेन मित्रतां स्वीकृतवान्। (a) What three things did the emperor do? (b) Why is the word निःशर्तम् important? (c) Why could Viravarman now accept what he had earlier refused? (d) What does समभावेन tell us about how he accepted?
questions.answer: (a) The emperor himself went to the forest, returned the kingdom unconditionally, and asked for friendship. (b) निःशर्तम् ('without condition') is crucial: earlier every gift was chained to दासभाव; now nothing degrading is attached, so accepting costs no dignity. (c) His objection had never been to wealth or to the emperor, only to servitude; once the condition vanished, acceptance was consistent with his principle — proof that his refusal was self-respect, not stubbornness or hatred of the emperor. (d) समभावेन ('with equanimity, as an equal') shows he accepted without gloating over his moral victory and without servile gratitude — the same even-mindedness he showed in hardship, now shown in triumph.
questions.explanation: The resolution: unconditional restoration lets dignity and acceptance coexist; equanimity in victory completes the portrait.

questions.question: Read the verse and answer: कुसुमस्तबकस्येव द्वयी वृत्तिर्मनस्विनः । मूर्ध्नि वा सर्वलोकस्य शीर्यते वन एव वा ॥ (a) Who is compared to what? (b) What are the two वृत्ति (courses)? (c) Which third possibility is silently excluded, and why does that exclusion carry the verse's message? (d) Give the meaning of मूर्ध्नि.
questions.answer: (a) The मनस्वी — the high-minded, self-respecting person — is compared to a कुसुमस्तबक, a cluster of flowers. (b) Either it rests on the head of the whole world (सर्वलोकस्य मूर्ध्नि) — full honour — or it withers away in the forest (वने शीर्यते) — dignified obscurity. (c) Excluded is the middle fate: lying trampled underfoot, half-used and degraded. That exclusion is the message — the self-respecting person accepts hardship and even obscurity, but never a life of humiliation under others' feet. (d) मूर्ध्नि = 'on the head' (locative of मूर्धन्).
questions.explanation: The simile's force lies in what it rules out: there is no third, trampled option for the मनस्वी.

questions.question: Read the verse and answer: गुणैरुत्तमतां याति नोच्चैरासनसंस्थितः । प्रासादशिखरस्थोऽपि काकः किं गरुडायते ॥ (a) State the general rule of the first line. (b) Explain the example of the second line. (c) How does this verse rebuke false pride of position? (d) Split the sandhi in प्रासादशिखरस्थोऽपि.
questions.answer: (a) Rule: one attains greatness by virtues (गुणैः), not by occupying a high seat (उच्चैः आसनसंस्थितः). (b) Example: a crow may perch on the very top of a palace, yet it does not thereby become Garuda, the king of birds — height of perch cannot change worth. (c) The verse rebukes those whose 'honour' rests on post, seat or status: position without merit is the crow on the tower — outer elevation, inner sameness; conversely, merit needs no throne to be great (Viravarman was great even in the forest). (d) प्रासादशिखरस्थोऽपि = प्रासादशिखरस्थः + अपि (विसर्ग-सन्धि; the elided अ is marked by the avagraha ऽ).
questions.explanation: Merit versus position; the crow-Garuda image and its sandhi.

questions.question: Case: रमेशः, a talented senior-secondary student, is offered the class-monitor post if he agrees to falsely report on a classmate the teacher dislikes. His friends say, 'Refuse rudely and walk out — show your honour!' Using the chapter, answer: (a) Should Ramesh accept the post? Why not? (b) Is the friends' advice स्वाभिमान? (c) What would a वीरवर्मा-like response look like? (d) Which verse best supports your answer?
questions.answer: (a) No. The post is offered at the price of an unjust act (false reporting) — like Chandasena's kingdom, it is advancement bought by selling integrity, and so is servitude, not honour. (b) No; rudeness is not self-respect. Insulting the teacher would be ego answering ego (अहङ्कार). Dignity refuses the condition, not the person's dignity. (c) A Viravarman-like response: decline firmly and politely — 'I respect you, but I cannot report falsely on anyone' — and accept the consequence (losing the post) with a calm face, as he accepted the forest. (d) Best support: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणाः... — let others blame or praise, let advantage come or go, the steadfast do not swerve a step from the just path. (गुणैरुत्तमतां याति also applies: the post without integrity is the crow on the tower.)
questions.explanation: Applies the offer-refusal pattern, the courtesy test, and the just-path verse to a school situation.

questions.question: Case: सीता accidentally damages her classmate's notebook. The classmate demands an apology before the class. Sita thinks, 'I am the topper — apologising publicly is beneath my honour.' Her friend गीता says, 'True honour can say sorry.' Using the chapter: (a) Whose view matches स्वाभिमान and whose matches अहङ्कार? (b) Which incident of the story settles the question? (c) What test from the chapter applies here? (d) What should Sita do?
questions.answer: (a) Gita's view matches स्वाभिमान — true self-respect includes giving others their due dignity; Sita's view ('beneath my honour') is अहङ्कार, honour misdefined as never bending. (b) The farmer incident settles it: Viravarman, a king, himself begged pardon of a poor farmer for damage his horse caused, and gave his last ring — apology after a genuine fault is the conduct of the truly self-respecting. (c) The apology test: self-respect can say 'I was wrong'; arrogance cannot. Also the root test: her refusal protects ego (status as topper), not any value — so it fails the just-path criterion. (d) Sita should apologise sincerely (and make good the damage if possible); far from lowering her, the apology will prove her dignity, as Viravarman's apology raised him even in the emperor's eyes.
questions.explanation: The farmer episode plus the apology test resolve a everyday school conflict.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: वीरवर्मा स्वाभिमानी आसीत्, न तु अहङ्कारी। सः वृद्धं गुरुं दृष्ट्वा प्रणमति स्म, कुम्भकारं कृषकं च आदरेण सम्भाषते स्म। (a) Translate both sentences into English. (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of: वृद्धम्, प्रणमति स्म, आदरेण. (c) Which two ordinary workers are named? (d) What contrast do the words 'न तु' mark?
questions.answer: (a) Translation: 'Viravarman was self-respecting, but not arrogant. Seeing his aged teacher he used to bow, and he used to speak with respect to the potter and the farmer.' (b) वृद्धम् = aged/old; प्रणमति स्म = used to bow (स्म with present = habitual past); आदरेण = with respect. (c) The potter (कुम्भकारः) and the farmer (कृषकः). (d) 'न तु' ('but not') marks the chapter's central contrast: स्वाभिमानी versus अहङ्कारी — the sentence affirms the first and denies the second of the same man.
questions.explanation: Translation, vocabulary, and the grammatical marker of the mana-ahankara contrast.
